newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss 1997 budget passes final hurdle.
newsitem.headline: Swiss 1997 budget passes final hurdle.

text.p: Switzerland's parliament on Tuesday gave final approval to a federal budget for 1997 with a deficit of 5.77 billion Swiss francs despite cost-cutting efforts.
The deficit is slightly more than a shortfall of 5.53 billion proposed by the cabinet and higher than a budgeted 1996 deficit of 4.05 billion Swiss francs.

The biggest single increase by parliament in 1997 spending was an extra 450 million Swiss francs for unemployment insurance as it became clear that joblessness could hover near a post-war annual high of five percent due to a stagnent economy.
Boosting unemployment coffers wiped out savings made by both chambers with a string of smaller cutbacks.
The Swiss federal budget has less of a market impact than those in other industrialised countries because of the relatively large volume of finance at the cantonal and local community level.

The 1996 deficit was based on planned revenue of 39.92 billion and expenditures of 43.97 billion, although spending has since been raised by 1.4 billion and the actual balance will not be known until early 1997.
The original Federal Council (cabinet) draft for 1997 foresaw spending of 43.9 billion and revenue of 38.4 billion.
Parliament's two chambers agreed to raise expenditures a total of about 250 million to 44.24 billion Swiss francs while leaving the revenue side untouched.
Parliament also approved a measure empowering the cabinet to borrow about 500 million Swiss francs for additional spending it can release during the year if Swiss economic growth is too slow.

The 1997 budget is based on government projections of 1.5 percent real economic growth and the deficit could swell as high as seven billion if the economy remains stagnant next year, Finance Minister Kaspar Villiger has said.
Government economic advisors this week forecast growth of only 0.5 percent in 1997 and a decline of 0.7 percent in this year's Gross Domestic Product.
GDP rose only 0.1 percent in 1995 and the economy has been roughly unchanged on average since 1991.
